items.title: The Lighthouse Keeper
items.text: Every evening at dusk, Tomas climbed the one hundred and twelve steps to the lamp room, just as his father had done before him. The sea below was the colour of slate, and the wind pulled at his coat as if it wanted him to hurry. He did not hurry. Years of practice had taught him that the lamp, like a nervous horse, must be approached slowly and with a steady hand. Tonight the new harbour lights glittered across the bay, brighter and cheaper than anything his lamp could offer, and the ferry captains no longer looked up at his tower. Tomas lit the flame anyway. "Somebody might still need it," he muttered, and he watched the beam sweep over the empty water, patient and faithful, like a promise nobody had asked him to keep.

qs.q: What is the passage mainly about?
o: A man who keeps doing his duty although it is no longer valued
A young sailor who loses his way in a dangerous winter storm at sea
A ferry company that plans to build a brand-new harbour
A father who is teaching his son how to repair a lamp
qs.why: Tomas continues to light the lamp even though the new harbour lights have made it unnecessary, so the passage is about faithful duty.

qs.q: Why have the ferry captains stopped looking up at the tower?
o: The old lamp has become too dim to be seen from the bay.
The new harbour lights now do the lamp's job for them.
Tomas has asked them to stay away from the rocks.
The captains are afraid of the wind near the cliffs.
qs.why: The text says the new harbour lights are brighter and cheaper than the lamp, so the captains no longer rely on it.

qs.q: In the passage, the word "faithful" is closest in meaning to
o: curious
loyal
cheerful
careless
qs.why: "Faithful" describes something that stays true to its duty, so it means loyal.

qs.q: What is the tone of the final sentence?
o: Angry and bitter about being replaced
Playful and full of jokes about the sea
Quietly sad, yet respectful of Tomas's devotion
Cold and unconcerned about what happens to the lamp next
qs.why: The simile of a promise nobody asked him to keep is gentle and sad, but it also admires his loyalty.

items.title: Morning Market
items.text:
Before the sun has cleared the roofs,
the awnings snap open like green wings.
A woman stacks her oranges in pyramids,
each one a small lamp lit for the day.
Fish lie silver on their beds of ice,
their round eyes full of last night's sea.
A boy runs past with bread held high,
a trophy warm against his chest.
The air is thick with mint and smoke
and prices called in a dozen tongues.
Nobody here is standing still;
even the pigeons seem to haggle.
Then comes the bell from the church tower,
and for a moment all the noise
folds down, as if the street itself
were taking one long breath
before it starts to sing again.

qs.q: "each one a small lamp lit for the day" compares the oranges to lamps. What does this metaphor suggest?
o: They are heavy and hard to carry
They are bright and add warmth to the scene
They are very expensive for most of the buyers in the market
They will not last until the evening
qs.why: A lamp gives light and warmth, so the metaphor shows the bright colour of the oranges.

qs.q: Which sense does the line "The air is thick with mint and smoke" appeal to most?
o: Smell
Hearing
Touch
Taste
qs.why: Mint and smoke are known by their scent, so the image appeals mainly to the sense of smell.

qs.q: Which line is an example of personification?
o: the awnings snap open like green wings
A boy runs past with bread held high
even the pigeons seem to haggle
Fish lie silver on their beds of ice
qs.why: Pigeons are given the human habit of bargaining over prices, which is personification. The other lines use a simile, plain description, or a metaphor.

qs.q: What happens when the church bell rings?
o: The market closes and the sellers go home.
The noise stops for a moment before life continues.
The boy drops his bread in the street and begins to cry loudly.
The fish are sold quickly to the first buyers.
qs.why: The street "folds down" its noise for a moment, as if taking a breath, and then it "starts to sing again".

items.title: The Heron and the Pond
items.text: A grey heron lived beside a pond so clear that every pebble on the bottom could be counted. For many years she caught a fish whenever she was hungry, and she was content. Then one summer she grew proud. "Small fish are beneath me," she said, and she refused them. She waited for a large, golden carp instead. Days passed. The small fish swam past her legs and laughed quietly, and still she waited. When the carp finally appeared, it was too quick and too clever, and it slipped away into deep water. By autumn the pond had grown cold, the small fish had hidden in the mud, and the heron stood alone on one thin leg, hungrier than she had ever been. Her pride, it seemed, had been the only meal she had eaten.

qs.q: Which lesson does this fable teach?
o: Clever animals always win in the end.
Being too proud can make us lose what we have.
Large fish are easier to catch than small ones.
Autumn is the hardest season for hunting.
qs.why: The heron's pride makes her refuse small fish and end up with nothing, so the moral is about the cost of pride.

qs.q: How is the passage organised?
o: It begins with a problem and then shows exactly how the heron solves it.
It shows a calm situation, a change in attitude, and a harsh result.
It compares two ponds and says which one is better.
It tells the story backward, starting from the ending.
qs.why: The heron is content, becomes proud, and then suffers; this is a sequence of situation, turning point, and result.

qs.q: What does the last sentence mean by "Her pride... had been the only meal she had eaten"?
o: She had actually eaten her own pride on that cold afternoon in autumn.
She had received nothing from her choices except pride.
She had enjoyed several meals of pride.
She was proud of the meal she had caught.
qs.why: It is a figure of speech: the only thing she gained was pride, which cannot feed her.

qs.q: Why did the small fish "laugh quietly"?
o: They found it funny that she ignored them while waiting for a carp.
They were about to be caught by the heron and were afraid of her.
They were telling each other a joke about the carp in the deep water.
They were happy that autumn was coming.
qs.why: The heron looked down on them and waited for the carp, so the small fish found her behaviour funny and safe for them.

items.title: A Letter to My Younger Sister
items.text:
Dear Mina,

By the time you read this, you will have unpacked your boxes and found out that the dormitory radiator makes a noise like an angry cat. Do not be discouraged. I remember my own first week at university: I ate lunch alone, I got lost twice a day, and I wrote home every night to say I wanted to come back. Mother kept all of those letters, and last month she showed them to me. I laughed until I cried, because the girl who wrote them seemed so far away.

I am not telling you this to make you feel better, though I hope it does. I am telling you because nobody told me. Be patient with yourself, and open your door sometimes. People will knock.

With love,
Joo-won

qs.q: What is the main purpose of this letter?
o: To describe the writer's own university courses in detail
To warn Mina about problems with the dormitory building
To comfort and encourage Mina as she begins a new life
To ask Mina to send news back to the family
qs.why: The writer shares her own difficult first week to reassure Mina that the beginning is hard but gets better.

qs.q: Why did Joo-won laugh until she cried when she read her old letters?
o: Her younger self seemed very distant from who she is now.
The letters were full of silly jokes about the noisy radiator and her roommates.
Her mother had changed the words as a prank.
She had forgotten how to write in her own language.
qs.why: She says the girl who wrote the letters "seemed so far away", showing how much she has changed.

qs.q: Which of the following is stated in the letter?
o: Mina's dormitory room has no radiator.
Joo-won once wrote home every night during her first week.
Their mother has thrown away the old letters.
Joo-won ate lunch with many new friends on her very first day at university.
qs.why: The letter says she "wrote home every night" to say she wanted to come back.

qs.q: The sentence "People will knock" suggests that
o: noisy neighbours will complain about Mina
Mina should expect new friends to come to her
the radiator will need to be repaired soon
visitors will interrupt Mina's studies very often in the evening
qs.why: After telling Mina to open her door, the writer promises that others will come to her, meaning friendship will follow.

items.title: The Kitchen Table (a scene)
items.text:
SETTING: A small kitchen, late at night. A single lamp is on. HANA sits at the table with a pile of unopened envelopes. HER BROTHER, JIN, enters in his pyjamas.

JIN: (yawning) You are still awake?

HANA: (not looking up) Someone has to pay the bills.

JIN: (sitting down) We could do it together tomorrow.

HANA: (pushing an envelope towards him) You said that last week. And the week before.

(A long pause. The clock ticks. JIN picks up the envelope and turns it over, as if the paper might bite.)

JIN: (quietly) I did not want to see how bad it was.

HANA: (softening) Neither did I. That is why I could not sleep.

(She slides a second envelope across the table. This time, he opens it.)

qs.q: What is the function of the stage directions in brackets?
o: They give the actors' real names and ages.
They tell how lines are spoken and what the characters do.
They summarise the whole plot of the play.
They explain difficult words and old customs to the audience in the theatre.
qs.why: Stage directions describe tone and action, such as "yawning" or "softening", so that the scene can be performed.

qs.q: What conflict is shown at the start of the scene?
o: Hana and Jin are arguing loudly about who owns the kitchen table.
Hana is annoyed because Jin has put off an unpleasant task.
Jin is angry that Hana has woken him in the night.
Both are afraid of a noise outside the house.
qs.why: Hana says Jin has promised to help for weeks and has not, so the tension comes from avoidance.

qs.q: Why does Jin turn the envelope over "as if the paper might bite"?
o: He wants to check whether it has been opened before.
He is afraid of what the bill will show.
He thinks the paper is torn at one corner.
He is looking for a name on the back.
qs.why: The simile suggests he fears bad news, which he confirms when he says he did not want to see how bad it was.

qs.q: What does the final stage direction suggest about Jin?
o: He is ready to face the problem with his sister.
He is going to leave the room in anger and go back to bed.
He has decided to ignore the bills again.
He is falling asleep at the table.
qs.why: By opening the envelope, Jin takes the first step to share the responsibility.

items.title: From a Winter Diary
items.text:
3 December. Snow fell all night, and when I opened the curtains this morning the garden had vanished. The bench, the apple tree, even the old wheelbarrow had been wrapped in white as carefully as presents. For a few minutes I forgot the cold, forgot the exam on Friday, forgot that my grandfather's chair has been empty since October. I just stood there with my breath making small clouds against the glass.

Then Mum called me for breakfast, and the ordinary day rushed back in. But something small had changed. I think I understood, for the first time, why Grandfather used to say that silence is not the absence of sound but the presence of attention. This morning I was paying attention, and the world was kind enough to reward me.

qs.q: What is the writer's main experience in this entry?
o: A brief moment of calm and awareness in the snowy garden
A frightening night spent alone in a cold and empty old house
A quarrel with a parent over the exam
A long walk to a faraway village
qs.why: The entry centres on the quiet moment at the window, when the writer pays attention to the beautiful scene.

qs.q: The phrase "wrapped in white as carefully as presents" is an example of
o: a simile
a contradiction
a rhyme
an exaggeration
qs.why: The snow-covered objects are compared to presents using "as... as", which is a simile.

qs.q: What can be inferred about the writer's grandfather?
o: He has recently died.
He lives in a different country.
He is angry about the exam.
He is waiting in the kitchen.
qs.why: His chair "has been empty since October" and the writer remembers his sayings in the past tense, so he has likely passed away.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the writer's insight?
o: Cold weather helps people to concentrate on their studies at home.
Quiet moments can be full of meaning if we notice them.
Gifts are more precious when they are wrapped well.
Old sayings are usually wrong about the world.
qs.why: The grandfather's saying about attention helps the writer understand that silence has value when we are attentive.

items.title: Autumn Leaf
items.text:
I am the last one on the branch,
a small brass coin of summer,
and the wind keeps asking for me
in a voice both rough and kind.
My sisters left in October,
spinning down like paper dancers.
They did not look back at the tree
that had held them through the rain.

Now I hang on, thin and bright,
while the sky turns the colour of ash.
Below, the children kick my sisters
into heaps and shout with joy.
Perhaps that is a kind of ending too:
to be the thing that someone leaps in.
The wind asks again. I loosen my fingers,
and the whole cold world rushes up to meet me.

qs.q: Who is the speaker of the poem?
o: A child playing in the park
The tree that lost its leaves
A leaf that is still on the branch
The wind blowing through the garden
qs.why: The speaker calls itself "the last one on the branch" and refers to "my sisters", so it is a leaf.

qs.q: "a small brass coin of summer" is a metaphor that suggests the leaf is
o: small, shiny and golden in colour
heavy and likely to break
noisy and difficult to ignore
dull, grey and ready to be thrown away
qs.why: A brass coin is small, shiny and yellow-gold, so the metaphor describes the leaf's size and bright colour.

qs.q: What do the last two lines suggest about the leaf's attitude toward falling?
o: It is terrified and tries hard to hold on to the branch.
It accepts the fall with calm and courage.
It is angry with the wind for calling.
It feels nothing at all.
qs.why: The leaf "loosens its fingers" and the whole world rushes up to meet it, showing willing acceptance.

qs.q: In the second stanza, how does the poem look at the fallen leaves?
o: As rubbish that spoils the ground
As a sign that the tree is unhealthy
As something that still brings happiness to children
As a warning of a long and cruel winter for the whole town
qs.why: The children shout with joy as they kick the leaves, so falling leaves still bring delight, which is a gentler view of ending.

items.title: The Cracked Cup
items.text:
Grandmother's blue cup sat at the back of the cupboard, and no one was allowed to use it. It had a thin crack running from the rim to the handle, like a river on a map. Clara had always wondered why it was kept at all.

On the morning of her departure for the city, Grandmother took the cup down, filled it with tea, and set it before her. "Drink," she said. Clara did, and the warm tea began to seep, very slowly, through the crack. By the time she reached the bottom, a small dark stain had spread across the saucer.

"You see?" said Grandmother, smiling. "It leaks. But it has never once been empty when I needed it." Clara said nothing. She only held the cup a little more tightly.

qs.q: What does the cracked cup most likely symbolise?
o: Something imperfect that is still deeply valuable
A gift that was bought in a faraway city by her uncle
A danger that Clara must avoid at all costs
A mistake that Grandmother wants to hide
qs.why: The cup leaks but is never empty when needed; it stands for flawed but faithful care, perhaps Grandmother herself.

qs.q: Which event first breaks the opening situation, in which nobody is allowed to use the cup?
o: Clara wonders why the cup is kept at the back of the cupboard.
Grandmother fills the cup and gives it to Clara.
The stain spreads over the saucer.
Clara goes to the city by train.
qs.why: Grandmother takes the forbidden cup down and fills it for Clara, which ends the opening situation and leads to the lesson.

qs.q: Why does Clara hold the cup "a little more tightly" at the end?
o: She is afraid that it will fall from her hands.
She has understood something moving about the cup.
She wants to take it with her without asking.
She is angry that the tea has leaked onto the clean saucer.
qs.why: Her silence and tighter grip show she is moved; she has grasped what the cup means to Grandmother.

qs.q: What is the effect of the simile "like a river on a map"?
o: It shows that the crack is thin but long and winding.
It proves that Grandmother is very good at drawing maps.
It suggests the cup came from another country.
It makes the crack seem dangerous to everyone.
qs.why: A river on a map is a thin winding line, which matches the crack from rim to handle.

items.title: Why Read Stories?
items.text: People sometimes ask what the use of fiction is. After all, the characters never lived and the events never happened. Yet I would argue that stories are among the most practical tools we own. A good novel lets us stand, for a few hundred pages, inside a mind that is not our own. We feel the shame of a boy who cannot read, or the fear of a woman crossing a border at night, and then we close the book and carry that borrowed feeling back into our own lives. In this way, fiction trains the imagination that kindness depends on. It is true that a story cannot repair a bridge or cure a fever. But a society that has forgotten how to imagine its neighbours will, sooner or later, stop building bridges for them.

qs.q: What is the writer's main argument?
o: Fiction is useful because it trains us to understand other people.
Novels are more accurate than newspapers and give better facts.
Readers should avoid stories about unhappy people.
Bridges should be built by writers rather than by trained engineers.
qs.why: The writer says stories train the imagination that kindness depends on, which makes them practical.

qs.q: Why does the writer say "a story cannot repair a bridge or cure a fever"?
o: To admit the limits of fiction before making a further point
To show that the writer dislikes both science and modern medicine
To suggest that doctors read too little
To warn readers against dangerous bridges
qs.why: The sentence concedes what fiction cannot do and then adds a deeper claim about imagining neighbours.

qs.q: In the passage, "borrowed feeling" refers to
o: a feeling taken from a character's experience
an emotion that a friend gave back
money lent by a library
an idea that is taken from another writer without permission
qs.why: The reader feels the character's shame or fear and brings that feeling into his or her own life, so it is a feeling borrowed from the story.

qs.q: What is the likely effect of the last sentence on the reader?
o: It makes the reader laugh at the idea of bridges.
It gives a warning that links imagination to social care.
It changes the topic from fiction to the work of engineers.
It repeats the first sentence in other words.
qs.why: The final sentence warns that without imagination people stop caring for others, and it ties the essay together.

items.title: The Sewing Machine
items.text:
The machine arrived in a wooden crate, scratched and smelling of oil. Soo-ah's grandmother had used it for forty years, and now it belonged to her.

She set it on the desk and turned the wheel. Suddenly she was seven again, lying on the floor of the old apartment while the needle chattered above her like a small, busy bird. Her grandmother had been hemming school uniforms, and every few minutes she would stop to bite a thread and say, "Never trust a straight line you did not draw yourself."

Now the apartment was gone, and so was the voice. Soo-ah threaded the needle on her third try and pressed the pedal. The machine coughed, hesitated, and began to sing. She did not stop until the first uneven seam was finished, crooked and perfect.

qs.q: Which narrative technique does the second paragraph use?
o: A flashback to the past
A prediction of the future
A change of narrator
A direct question to the reader
qs.why: Soo-ah remembers being seven years old, so the story moves back in time with a flashback.

qs.q: What does the phrase "crooked and perfect" suggest?
o: The seam is flawed, but it matters deeply to Soo-ah.
The seam is exactly straight, as if drawn with a ruler tool.
The machine is broken beyond repair.
Soo-ah has no wish to sew again.
qs.why: A crooked seam is imperfect, yet it is perfect for her because it continues her grandmother's work, so the contradiction is intended.

qs.q: The needle is compared to "a small, busy bird" because
o: it moves quickly and makes light, repeated sounds
it flies about the room in the night
it hurts the small child who is lying on the floor below
it is coloured like a feathered animal
qs.why: The comparison shows the speed and the chattering sound of the needle.

qs.q: What is the mood of the final paragraph?
o: Tender and quietly hopeful
Frightened, tense and unsure
Bitter and resentful
Silly and playful
qs.why: Soo-ah's effort and the machine beginning to "sing" create a warm, moving mood of continuing a loved one's memory.

items.title: City Rain
items.text:
The rain comes down on the city street
with a thousand tiny feet,
tapping the roofs and the parking meters,
drumming the taxis in the heat
that lingers from the day.
The gutters gargle, the windows blur,
and the neon signs begin to stir
and bleed their colours into the road
like paint in a glass of water.

A man with a newspaper over his head
runs for the bus. A dog stands still,
content to be soaked. The shop girl smiles
at nothing, at the grey, at the thrill
of being out of reach for a while.
And I, at the window, with my cold tea,
think how the whole loud city
has been told to slow down, and has agreed.

qs.q: What do "a thousand tiny feet" represent?
o: The raindrops hitting the ground
The crowd of people running home
The paws of stray animals in the street
The wheels of passing taxis
qs.why: The raindrops are imagined as tiny feet tapping on roofs and meters; the line is a metaphor.

qs.q: Which line contains a simile?
o: the whole loud city has been told to slow down
The gutters gargle, the windows blur
and bleed their colours into the road like paint in a glass of water
A dog stands still, content to be soaked
qs.why: The neon colours spreading in the wet road are compared to paint in water using "like".

qs.q: What is the speaker's feeling about the rain?
o: Calm appreciation for the way it slows the city
Strong anger at the damage that the storm causes
Fear of being alone in the room
Disappointment that the day is spoiled
qs.why: The speaker watches from the window and enjoys the city's slowing, as the last lines show.

qs.q: The poem mentions the shop girl smiling "at nothing". This suggests that
o: she is making fun of the customers who come to the shop
the rain has put people into a lighter, dreamy mood
she has lost her job
she is confused by the noise
qs.why: She smiles without a clear reason, which shows the rain's soft effect on the mood of the city.

items.title: The Umbrella
items.text:
Mr. Park had saved for six months to buy his wife a silver umbrella for her birthday. It was slim and elegant, with a handle shaped like a swan's neck. She had admired it in a shop window every Tuesday since spring.

On the morning of the birthday, he wrapped it in tissue paper and tied a ribbon around it. At the same moment, his wife was in the next room, wrapping a small box for him. Inside was a leather case for his old reading glasses, bought with the money from selling her winter coat.

It rained all afternoon. They ate dinner, exchanged their presents, and laughed, and then, a little embarrassed, both fell silent. He had no need of a case; he had lost his glasses on Monday. And on a day like this, she now had no coat to wear under her new umbrella.

qs.q: What literary device is the main feature of the ending?
o: Situational irony
Alliteration of sounds
Onomatopoeia
Rhymed verse
qs.why: Each person sacrifices something for a gift that has become useless, which is the opposite of what was intended: situational irony.

qs.q: What can be inferred about the couple?
o: They love each other but have little money.
They are rich and love to compete.
They dislike giving and receiving gifts on special days.
They often quarrel about money.
qs.why: Saving for six months and selling a coat show that they care about one another and have few resources.

qs.q: Why did the couple become "a little embarrassed"?
o: They saw that their gifts no longer matched their needs.
They had forgotten the date of the birthday until the evening.
They were afraid that the guests would arrive much too early.
They found the presents were too cheap.
qs.why: The case is useless without glasses, and the umbrella cannot make up for the coat she sold, so the sacrifices cancelled each other out.

qs.q: What does the story mainly suggest about gifts?
o: The love behind a gift matters more than its use.
Gifts should always be bought in shops, never made by hand.
It is better to give money than objects.
Rain spoils all celebrations.
qs.why: Despite the awkward result, the couple's willingness to sacrifice shows the value of love and care.

items.title: The Moon Merchant
items.text:
In a village at the foot of the mountains, there was once a merchant who claimed that he could sell the moon. Every night he set up a stall, filled a large bowl with water, and invited the villagers to look. The moon trembled in the water, round and white. "Ten coins for a night's loan," he said, and many people paid, for the water seemed to hold a beauty that the sky could not.

One night a little girl named Seon leaned over the bowl and said, "But the moon is above us. You are only selling its reflection." The crowd murmured. The merchant did not argue. He simply tipped the bowl onto the road, and the moon disappeared. "Then look up," he said gently, "and keep your coins." From that day the villagers watched the sky for free, and they say the moon has never looked brighter.

qs.q: What happens at the climax of the tale?
o: The girl names the truth and the merchant ends his trick.
The merchant sells the moon to a rich visitor from the capital.
The villagers chase the merchant out of town.
The bowl is stolen by a stranger.
qs.why: The girl's remark is the point of greatest tension, and the merchant's reaction resolves the story.

qs.q: Which theme does the tale express?
o: True beauty is free to anyone who looks in the right place.
Children should never speak to merchants who sell by moonlight.
Water is more valuable than silver.
Mountains protect villages from thieves.
qs.why: The villagers learn that they can enjoy the real moon for free by looking up, so the theme is about true beauty.

qs.q: What is the merchant's attitude at the end?
o: Gentle and wise, though he loses his income
Furious at being exposed in front of the village
Afraid of the villagers
Proud of his fine trick
qs.why: He speaks "gently" and tells them to keep their coins, which shows grace in defeat.

qs.q: "the moon has never looked brighter" is the narrator's way of showing that
o: people now appreciate what was always there
the weather has turned warmer
the water in the bowl was very clean
the merchant has made the moon larger and brighter
qs.why: The change is in the villagers' attention and appreciation, not in the moon itself.

items.title: The Gardener Robot
items.text:
Unit 7 had tended the rooftop garden for eleven years, but it had never been asked what it thought of tomatoes. When a small boy named Eli posed the question, the robot paused, its sensors whirring.

"I do not eat," it said at last. "I cannot taste. And yet, when the first red fruit appears, my processors run faster than they do for any other event. I do not know whether that is liking. Perhaps you can tell me."

Eli considered this seriously. "It sounds like liking to me," he said. "You wait for it, and you are happy when it comes."

The robot recorded the conversation in its memory and, for the first time in eleven years, labelled the file with a single word: "joy". Then it went back to the tomatoes, whose leaves were beginning, quietly, to turn.

qs.q: What question does this story raise?
o: Can a machine have feelings like humans do?
Why do tomatoes grow best on roofs in the city?
How long can a robot work without repairs?
Who should be in charge of the garden?
qs.why: Unit 7 cannot taste yet reacts strongly to the fruit; the boy suggests that this may be liking, so the story raises the question of machine feelings.

qs.q: Which words best describe Eli's reaction to the robot?
o: Thoughtful and kind
Frightened and impatient
Rude and bored
Amused and cruel
qs.why: He "considered this seriously" and gives a kind, helpful answer.

qs.q: Why does the robot label the file "joy"?
o: It has accepted Eli's idea about its own response.
It is following a rule written into its main program.
It wants to share the file with the boy.
It is trying to hide the information.
qs.why: After hearing Eli say it sounds like liking, the robot names its experience with a human word, joy.

qs.q: What is the effect of the final sentence?
o: It shows that life continues and time passes quietly.
It introduces a sudden danger that threatens the rooftop garden.
It suggests that the robot is about to break.
It begins a new conversation with Eli.
qs.why: Leaves beginning to turn hints at the change of season and the calm routine that carries on after the emotional moment.

items.title: First Day in a New Country
items.text:
On my first morning in Canada, my host mother handed me a mug of hot chocolate and said, "Make yourself at home." I stood in the kitchen, mug in hand, and did not know what to do. At home, a guest would never open a refrigerator in someone else's house. Here, apparently, that was exactly what "at home" meant. She laughed when I finally asked permission to take a glass of water, and she opened the fridge herself, saying that from now on I should help myself whenever I was thirsty.

It was a tiny moment, but I thought about it for days. Two families, two ways of showing care: one by never intruding, the other by inviting you to take. Neither is wrong. I only had to learn the language that the kindness was written in.

qs.q: Why did the writer hesitate in the kitchen?
o: She was taught that guests should not open a fridge uninvited.
She did not like hot chocolate very much.
She could not understand any English words.
She thought the host mother was angry with her for arriving late.
qs.why: In her own culture a guest does not open someone's fridge, so "make yourself at home" confused her.

qs.q: What is the writer's conclusion about the two customs?
o: Both are valid ways of expressing care.
The Canadian way is clearly better.
Her own custom is rude to hosts.
The difference is not worth thinking about.
qs.why: She says neither is wrong; they are different languages of kindness.

qs.q: What does "the language that the kindness was written in" mean?
o: The customs through which kindness is shown
The English words in the long letters from the host
A secret code between the two families
The grammar rules the writer studied
qs.why: It is a metaphor: kindness exists in every culture but is expressed through different customs that must be learned.

qs.q: The host mother opened the fridge herself in order to
o: show that the guest was truly welcome to help herself
look for something to cook for dinner
teach the writer a lesson about good manners at the table
hide food from the writer
qs.why: She wanted to make the guest feel at home and to show that taking a drink was fine.

items.title: The Missing Key
items.text:
The key was not on the hook. Inspector Hale knew this before he looked, because the hook had a clean circle of dust around it, the sort that appears only when something hangs there for years and is suddenly taken away.

"The housekeeper says she last saw it on Tuesday," said the young constable.

"The housekeeper says a great many things." Hale crouched by the cellar door and ran a finger along the lock. There were no scratches. Whoever had opened it had come with the key, and not just any key; the right one. He straightened up, frowning at the dim hall. Somebody in this house, he suspected, had practised walking quietly down these stairs, and had been rehearsing for rather longer than one night.

qs.q: Which part of a story does this passage represent?
o: The exposition that introduces a mystery
The final resolution of all questions
The reflection of the narrator many years later
A description of the setting without any conflict
qs.why: A crime is introduced, clues are seen, and no solution has yet been reached, so this is an opening that sets up the mystery.

qs.q: What does the lack of scratches on the lock suggest?
o: The person who opened the door had the real key.
The lock was replaced only a few weeks ago by the housekeeper.
The door was never locked at all.
A thief used a very sharp tool.
qs.why: The lock shows no signs of forced entry, so Hale concludes that the right key was used.

qs.q: What does the inspector suspect at the end?
o: The act was planned in advance by someone in the house.
The young constable has made a serious error in his report.
The housekeeper has left the country.
The cellar has been empty for years.
qs.why: "Rehearsing for rather longer than one night" suggests careful planning by a member of the household.

qs.q: The phrase "The housekeeper says a great many things" shows that Hale
o: does not fully trust what the housekeeper says
enjoys long conversations with her in the evening hall
wants to hire her as an assistant
is worried that she may be ill
qs.why: The remark is mildly sarcastic and suggests that her statements may not be reliable.

items.title: Mr. Alder the Baker
items.text:
Mr. Alder rose at three each morning, when the town was still a dark rumour, and by five his shop smelled of bread so rich that passers-by slowed down without knowing why. He was a large man with small, careful hands, and he handled dough the way other people handle sleeping babies. To the children he gave the crusts, which he claimed were the best part; to the lonely widows he gave the ends of the loaf and a remark about the weather, which was the best part for them.

He never advertised, and he never raised his prices. "Bread," he liked to say, "is not a business. It is a conversation that happens to end in breakfast." The accountants shook their heads. The town, however, kept him alive, which is the only sort of profit a baker can really spend.

qs.q: Which description best characterises Mr. Alder?
o: Generous and devoted to his craft
Greedy and careless
Shy and fearful of most of his customers
Lazy and forgetful
qs.why: He works hard at dawn, treats dough gently, and gives to children and widows.

qs.q: The comparison between dough and "sleeping babies" emphasises his
o: gentleness and care
speed and strength
ambition and cleverness
anger and impatience
qs.why: People handle sleeping babies very softly, so the simile shows his tenderness with dough.

qs.q: Why did the accountants "shake their heads"?
o: They thought his business methods made little financial sense.
They were annoyed by the smell of baking bread so early each morning.
They were too busy to eat breakfast.
They wanted to buy his shop.
qs.why: He did not advertise or raise prices, which seems unwise to people concerned with money.

qs.q: What is the meaning of "the only sort of profit a baker can really spend"?
o: The community's support is what supports his living.
He earns more money than other bakers.
He sells his bread at a very high price to rich customers.
He spends his profits on advertising.
qs.why: The town "kept him alive", meaning the customers' loyalty provided what he needed to live.

items.title: Four Seasons in Short
items.text:
Spring
Thin rain on the roof,
a green hum in the garden.
The earth clears her throat.

Summer
Cicadas shouting,
the road a shimmering sheet.
Even shade is hot.

Autumn
Red leaves on the stream
carry small boats to the sea.
Nobody sends word.

Winter
White fields, black branches.
The kettle starts to whisper.
Someone is coming.

(Four poems, each of three lines. The writer wrote them in a single week while recovering from an illness and looking out of a hospital window, where the only things to see were a plane tree, a bus stop and a strip of sky, so the seasons had to be imagined as much as seen.)

qs.q: Which line is an example of personification?
o: The earth clears her throat.
Thin rain on the roof
White fields, black branches.
Red leaves on the stream
qs.why: The earth is given a human action, clearing her throat, to suggest the first signs of spring.

qs.q: What is the effect of "Even shade is hot"?
o: It stresses how intense the summer heat is.
It shows that the writer likes sitting in the sun.
It suggests that trees have died.
It explains how shade is made.
qs.why: If even the cool shade feels hot, the heat must be extreme; this is a deliberate contradiction for effect.

qs.q: What mood does the winter poem create?
o: Quiet anticipation and warmth
Anger, noise and a sense of sudden fear
Complete despair
Silly excitement
qs.why: The whispering kettle and the line "Someone is coming" create a calm, warm feeling of waiting.

qs.q: What does the note in brackets add to our reading?
o: It hints that the poems show a patient's hopeful view.
It proves that all four poems are about illness.
It tells us that the writer is a famous doctor.
It explains how to write poems in three lines.
qs.why: Knowing the writer was recovering and looking out of a window helps explain the quiet watching and hope in the poems.

items.title: The Spelling Bee
items.text:
When the judge said "necessary", Dahye's mouth went dry. She had practised that word a hundred times, but the stage lights were hot and the audience was a dark wall of faces. "N-E-C," she began, and stopped. In the second row her father, who had never learned English properly, held up a card on which he had written one letter: the second S. He had copied it from her notebook the night before.

She could have laughed or cried. Instead she breathed, closed her eyes, and said, "N-E-C-E-S-S-A-R-Y."

The judge nodded. The room exploded in applause. Later, when reporters asked what she had been thinking, Dahye said only, "I was thinking about a card." Only her father understood why he was crying behind his programme.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
o: A girl succeeds with the quiet support of her father.
A judge makes a serious mistake with a very difficult word.
Reporters discover a secret about the contest.
A father teaches his daughter English at home.
qs.why: Dahye overcomes her fear with the help of her father's card, so the story is about support and courage.

qs.q: What does the father's card show about him?
o: He wants to help though he does not know English well.
He does not believe that Dahye can spell the word.
He disagrees with the judge's decision.
He is angry that Dahye is nervous.
qs.why: He copied the letter from her notebook, showing effort and love without strong English.

qs.q: Why does Dahye say, "I was thinking about a card"?
o: She thanks her father in a way only he understands.
She has forgotten the reporters' question.
She is trying to confuse the audience and the other contestants.
She hopes to win a prize for the card.
qs.why: Only her father understands the answer, so it is a private gesture of thanks.

qs.q: Which phrase best describes how the story ends?
o: Emotional and warm
Mysterious and dark
Bitter and cold
Silly and loud
qs.why: The applause, the quiet answer, and the father crying behind his programme create a moving, warm ending.

items.title: The Ferry (a scene)
items.text:
SETTING: The deck of a small ferry at dawn. Mist covers the water. OLD MAN LEE leans on the railing. A girl, YUNA, with a heavy rucksack, approaches him.

YUNA: (shyly) Is this the boat to the island?

LEE: (without turning) The only one. Are you running away or coming home?

YUNA: (surprised) Why do you ask?

LEE: Nobody carries a bag that heavy for a holiday. (He finally looks at her, kindly.) I have made this crossing for fifty years. People who run away look at the water. People who go home look at the horizon.

(YUNA turns to the horizon. A pause. The ferry horn sounds.)

YUNA: (softly) Then I suppose I am going home.

(LEE nods and offers her a cup from his flask. The sun begins to rise.)

qs.q: What can the audience infer from Lee's first question?
o: He can read people's situations from small signs.
He is the ferry's captain.
He is worried about the weather.
He wants to take Yuna's heavy bag for the whole crossing.
qs.why: He guesses her reason for travelling from her heavy bag, showing experience in reading people.

qs.q: What is the symbolic meaning of the sunrise at the end?
o: A new beginning and hope
A coming storm
The end of the story's setting
A warning for the passengers
qs.why: Sunrise at the moment she accepts she is going home symbolises renewal.

qs.q: Why does Yuna turn to the horizon?
o: She wants to find out what kind of traveller she is.
She hears a strange noise coming from the island in the mist.
She is trying to avoid Lee's flask.
She wants to take a photograph.
qs.why: Lee's remark makes her test herself: looking at the horizon suggests she is going towards something, not away from it.

qs.q: How do the stage directions help build the characters?
o: They show Yuna's shyness and Lee's gentle kindness.
They list the actors' costumes in great and careful detail.
They give historical facts about the ferry.
They state the ending of the play in advance.
qs.why: Words such as "shyly" and "kindly" reveal the manner of each character.

items.title: Crossing the Dunes
items.text:
The caravan had been walking since midnight. By noon the dunes rose on every side like a frozen sea, and the sun lay on the travellers' shoulders like a hand that refused to lift. No one spoke. Even the camels, usually so scornful, had lowered their heads and fallen into a steady, swaying silence.

Amira counted her steps to keep her mind from the water that was almost gone. Four hundred, she told herself, and then she would let herself look at the horizon. At four hundred, there was nothing. At eight hundred, nothing. At one thousand, something shimmered, green and impossibly small, and she wondered whether the desert had begun to play tricks.

Behind her, the old guide lifted his head and, for the first time that day, smiled.

qs.q: What is the mood of the opening paragraph?
o: Heavy, hot and exhausting
Cheerful, calm and relaxed
Funny and noisy
Cold and mysterious
qs.why: Images of a heavy sun, silence, and lowered heads create a draining mood.

qs.q: "the sun lay on the travellers' shoulders like a hand that refused to lift" is an example of
o: a simile with a sense of weight
an onomatopoeia
a rhyme scheme
a rhetorical question to the reader
qs.why: The sun is compared to a heavy hand using "like", and the image conveys the oppressive weight of the heat.

qs.q: What is Amira's reason for counting steps?
o: To distract herself from worry about water
To measure the size of the desert
To compete with the camels
To plan her route on a map of the whole desert
qs.why: She counts "to keep her mind from the water that was almost gone".

qs.q: Why does the guide smile at the end?
o: He realises the green shape means water is near.
He is pleased that Amira has finished counting.
He is glad that the camels have stopped walking.
He remembers a joke from his childhood.
qs.why: The green thing that shimmers is likely an oasis; the experienced guide would know this and smile with relief.

items.title: A Review of "The Salt Road"
items.text:
In her second novel, "The Salt Road", Helena Marsh follows a family of merchants through three generations, and the result is a book of unusual patience. Marsh refuses the easy thrills of her genre. There are no battles, no villains; instead, the tension comes from small decisions made over small meals. When a daughter chooses silence at the dinner table, an entire marriage trembles.

The prose can be demanding. Long, winding sentences sometimes lose the reader, and the middle section moves so slowly that I checked the page count more than once. Yet the final chapters repay every minute. The closing image, a grandmother rubbing salt from her palms onto a child's tongue, is one of the most moving things I have read this year. Not a perfect novel, but a memorable one.

qs.q: What is the reviewer's overall opinion of the novel?
o: Mostly positive, with some reservations
Completely negative
Fully positive, without a single word of criticism
Neutral and without any opinion
qs.why: The reviewer praises the patience and ending but also criticises the dense prose and slow middle.

qs.q: According to the review, what creates tension in the novel?
o: Small choices within the family
Violent fights between merchants
A mystery about a hidden treasure
Natural disasters on the road
qs.why: The review says there are no battles or villains; tension comes from small decisions at meals.

qs.q: What does the phrase "repay every minute" suggest?
o: The ending makes the long reading worthwhile.
The book must be returned to the library on time.
The reader should count each minute while reading.
The author is paid by the minute.
qs.why: Although the middle is slow, the final chapters reward the reader for his or her time.

qs.q: Which statement would the reviewer most likely agree with?
o: A book can be moving even if it is flawed.
Readers should avoid slow novels.
Long sentences are always an advantage to the reader.
Thrillers are better than family stories.
qs.why: "Not a perfect novel, but a memorable one" shows that flaws do not prevent a strong impact.

items.title: Why the Owl Hunts at Night
items.text:
In the early days of the world, the owl was the proudest bird of the forest, and her feathers shone like polished copper in the sun. All the other birds admired her, and she believed their admiration was her due. One spring, when the king of the birds called a meeting to choose who should guard the sleeping eggs, the owl alone refused to attend. "I do not take orders from creatures who sing so badly," she said.

The king answered her quietly. "Then you shall guard the dark hours, when nobody sings and nobody sees you. Perhaps there you will learn what it is to listen." From that day on, the owl hunted by night. They say that her round eyes grew large in the dark, and that she hears the smallest rustle, because she is still learning to listen.

qs.q: What problem begins the myth?
o: The owl is too proud to join the others.
The eggs are stolen by a hungry fox from the oak tree.
The king loses his crown.
The forest suffers from a long drought.
qs.why: The owl refuses to attend the meeting and insults the other birds, which causes the king's judgement.

qs.q: What is the purpose of this kind of story?
o: To explain how something in nature came to be
To give a scientific report on birds
To advertise a forest hotel
To describe a historical battle between two kingdoms
qs.why: It is a myth that gives an imaginative explanation for why the owl hunts at night and has large eyes.

qs.q: The king's punishment is best described as
o: a lesson that matches the owl's fault
a random act of anger
a reward for her bravery
a trick he plays on her in front of the others
qs.why: She would not listen, so she receives a life that teaches listening; the punishment fits the fault.

qs.q: In the sentence "she believed their admiration was her due", the phrase "her due" means
o: something she deserved
something she owed to the king
something she feared
something she stole
qs.why: "Due" here means what is rightfully owed to her; she thought she deserved the admiration.

items.title: The Parrot Who Told the Truth
items.text:
Madame Orlova's parrot had a talent that no one had asked for: he repeated everything he overheard. For years this was harmless, even charming. Visitors enjoyed hearing him imitate the doorbell, the kettle and the postman's cough.

Then came the dinner party. Madame had invited her richest neighbour, and she spent an hour describing how delighted she was to see him. The parrot, in the corner, listened to every compliment. Later that evening, just as the neighbour was lifting his dessert fork, the bird said in Madame's own voice, "What a bore he is! If only he would go home!"

The silence lasted nearly a minute. Madame turned the colour of her white tablecloth. The neighbour, to everyone's surprise, burst out laughing. "At last," he said, "an honest voice in this house." They became the closest of friends, and the parrot was given the best seat at every dinner.

qs.q: What is the humour in the story based on?
o: A creature repeats what was meant to be private.
A guest forgets his own name.
A servant breaks an expensive plate in the kitchen.
A host is late for her own party.
qs.why: The parrot repeats Madame's private insult at the worst possible time, which creates comic embarrassment.

qs.q: Why did the neighbour laugh?
o: He valued honesty more than polite flattery.
He did not understand a single word that the parrot said.
He wanted to hide his anger.
He planned to take the bird home.
qs.why: He called it "an honest voice", showing that he appreciated plain truth.

qs.q: What is the likely message of the story?
o: Honesty can build a deeper friendship than flattery.
Parrots should never be kept as pets.
Dinner parties are always dangerous.
Rich people prefer to be insulted by their closest friends.
qs.why: The friendship that results from the honest remark shows the value of sincerity.

qs.q: The phrase "Madame turned the colour of her tablecloth" suggests that she
o: went pale with shock
felt very proud
became extremely angry
began to feel sleepy
qs.why: A white tablecloth suggests she went pale from embarrassment or shock.

items.title: A Word for Home
items.text:
My grandmother, who has lived in three countries, says that there is no true translation of the word "home". In her first language it can mean a house, a village, a smell, even a particular song. In English, she complains, it sounds too much like a place on a map.

I used to think this was an old person's complaint. But last summer, living for six weeks in a flat with strangers, I noticed that I did not call it home until the evening a flatmate left the light on for me. Nothing else had changed: the sink still leaked, the walls were still thin. The word arrived with the light.

I now suspect my grandmother is right. A language gives us labels, but it is people who fill them.

qs.q: What is the writer's main point about the word "home"?
o: Its meaning depends on feeling more than on place.
It can be translated easily into every other language.
It describes only a house with a roof.
It is a word that old people use too often.
qs.why: The writer concludes that the word is filled by people and feelings, not only by geography.

qs.q: Why does the grandmother think English is lacking?
o: The English word seems to refer only to a location.
English has too many difficult sounds for most speakers.
English does not have a word for houses.
English speakers dislike travelling.
qs.why: She says "home" in English sounds too much like a place on a map.

qs.q: What caused the writer to feel the flat was home?
o: Someone's small act of thoughtfulness
Repairs made to the leaking kitchen sink
The thick walls that kept out noise
A letter from her grandmother
qs.why: The word came when a flatmate left the light on for her.

qs.q: The sentence "The word arrived with the light" is an example of
o: a figure of speech linking a feeling to a small event
a literal description of a parcel being delivered by post
a question put to the reader
a rhyme
qs.why: The word is treated as if it could arrive; the image links the sense of home to the kind gesture of the light.

items.title: Inheritance
items.text:
From my father I inherited a watch
that has not told the time for twenty years,
a pair of hands that fold the same way his did
when he was thinking, and a distrust of banks.

From my mother I inherited the habit
of keeping the radio on in an empty room,
so that the house will not feel abandoned,
and a way of saying "fine" that means the opposite.

Neither of them left me land or money.
The lawyer, when he read the will,
looked faintly sorry. I thanked him.
I did not tell him that I already held
everything they had ever owned
and that it fit, quite easily, inside a life.

I wind the watch. It does not move.
But the hands, when I look down, are theirs.

qs.q: What does the speaker mean by "it fit, quite easily, inside a life"?
o: Her parents left habits and memories, not things.
The speaker lives in a very small house in a crowded city.
The lawyer packed the parents' belongings neatly.
The speaker plans to sell the watch.
qs.why: The phrase suggests that the true inheritance is a way of living, which is carried inside the speaker.

qs.q: What does the broken watch symbolise?
o: The father's presence that remains after his death
A mistake the speaker made as a child in the old house
A modern gift from the lawyer
The speaker's fear of banks
qs.why: The watch no longer works but is treasured; it stands for the father's memory.

qs.q: What is the tone of the poem?
o: Quiet, affectionate and thoughtful
Furious, bitter and full of complaints
Joking and careless
Excited and loud
qs.why: The speaker lists small details of her parents with tenderness, without anger or noise.

qs.q: The phrase "a way of saying 'fine' that means the opposite" shows that the mother
o: hid her real feelings behind a short word
always told the exact truth
disliked the radio and the noise of the house
spoke very little English
qs.why: When she said "fine" she did not mean it, so she hid her troubles.

items.title: The Last Train
items.text:
The platform was empty except for a boy and an old woman at opposite ends. The clock above them said eleven fifty-two. Jun checked his phone again; the battery was at two per cent.

"It is not coming, you know," said the woman, without raising her voice. She seemed to speak to the rails. "They stopped the last train on Sundays years ago. I only come here to remember."

Jun looked at her properly. She wore a green coat that was too thin for the night. "What do you remember?" he asked, and was surprised to find that he truly wanted to know.

She told him about a young man, a suitcase, and a promise made on this very platform. By the time she finished, the phone had died, and Jun did not mind at all. They walked out together into the cold, sharing the long, slow business of a story.

qs.q: What is the central conflict at the beginning?
o: Jun is stranded and the train will not arrive.
Two travellers argue loudly about what the clock says.
The woman steals Jun's phone.
The station is being closed for repairs.
qs.why: He waits for a train that has stopped running, which creates the problem.

qs.q: How does Jun's attitude change during the passage?
o: From impatience to interest in another person
From calm to rage
From curiosity about the woman to fear of the dark
From joy to sadness
qs.why: He begins by checking his phone but ends up caring more about her story than about his own situation.

qs.q: Why does the woman come to the platform?
o: She comes to remember a promise from her past.
She works as a night guard at the quiet old station.
She wants to sell tickets to travellers.
She is waiting for Jun's phone call.
qs.why: She says "I only come here to remember" and then tells of a promise made there.

qs.q: The sentence "the long, slow business of a story" suggests that
o: telling and listening to a story takes time and care
stories are a kind of paid job for people at stations
the train is moving slowly
the woman is making up a lie
qs.why: The phrase presents the story as a patient shared activity.

items.title: Book Club: A Poem About a Bridge
items.text:
Nora: Did everyone read the poem about the old stone bridge?
Ben: I did, but I am not sure I understood it. It seems to be about a bridge, yet the speaker never crosses it.
Nora: That is exactly the point, I think. The bridge is more than stone. It is a symbol of a connection the speaker is afraid to make.
Ben: Hmm. I read it as a simple description of a quiet evening.
Mei: There are too many hints for that. The bridge is "worn by a thousand footsteps", but the speaker's shoes stay dry on the bank.
Ben: Fair enough. And the last line, "the river keeps what it cannot carry", is strange.
Mei: To me it means that some feelings are too heavy to cross over, so they stay behind.
Nora: I would add that the river is also a barrier. Water divides, while the bridge joins.
Ben: So the poem is about the wish to reach another person, and the fear of doing it.
Nora: Yes. Next time, shall we choose something more cheerful?
Mei: Only if you promise not to explain it all before I finish my tea.

qs.q: What is the group mainly doing in this conversation?
o: Interpreting the meaning of a poem together
Planning a long trip across an old stone bridge
Arguing about a river's name
Writing a poem as a team
qs.why: They exchange readings of the poem's symbols and decide what it means.

qs.q: According to Nora, the bridge in the poem is
o: a symbol of a connection the speaker fears to make
a plain description of a place the speaker likes to visit
a warning of a flood
a memory of the speaker's childhood
qs.why: Nora says the bridge stands for a connection that the speaker is afraid to make.

qs.q: Which detail does Mei use to support her view?
o: The speaker's shoes remain dry on the bank.
The poem has a regular rhyme scheme and a strict rhythm.
The speaker names the bridge's builder.
The poem was written long ago.
qs.why: She points to the contrast between the worn bridge and the dry shoes, which show the speaker never crosses.

qs.q: What does Ben finally conclude?
o: It is about wanting to reach someone and fearing to try.
The poem is only about stone and water.
The poem is too cheerful to analyse.
The poem should be removed from the group's reading list for good.
qs.why: Ben restates the group's reading in his last long turn.

qs.q: What is the tone of Mei's last remark?
o: Gently teasing
Deeply angry
Quite fearful
Formal and serious
qs.why: She jokes about Nora explaining everything, which is a friendly tease.

items.title: Teacher and Student: The Ending of a Story
items.text:
Teacher: You told me you were unhappy with the ending of "The Red Door". Why?
Jisoo: Because nothing is solved. The girl stands in front of the door and the story just stops.
Teacher: Do you think the author forgot to finish?
Jisoo: No, but it felt unfair. We followed her for twenty pages.
Teacher: Let us look at the last sentence together. She "put her hand on the handle and felt it turn". What is the author showing us?
Jisoo: That the door is not locked. It could open.
Teacher: And what has the story been about up to this point?
Jisoo: Her fear of leaving home.
Teacher: So the real question was never what is behind the door.
Jisoo: It was whether she would try the handle. Oh. So the story is complete after all.
Teacher: An open ending asks the reader to do some of the work. Whether you like it is a separate matter.

qs.q: Why was Jisoo unhappy with the ending at first?
o: She felt nothing was resolved.
She thought the story was too long.
She did not understand the vocabulary.
She disliked the main character's name.
qs.why: She says nothing is solved and the story stops.

qs.q: What does the detail of the handle turning show?
o: The girl has taken the step that matters.
The door is broken and cannot be opened by her.
Someone is on the other side.
The story will continue next week.
qs.why: The turn of the handle shows she takes action, which answers the real question of whether she dares to leave.

qs.q: What does the teacher mean by an "open ending"?
o: One that leaves some meaning to the reader
One that has exactly twenty pages
One that explains every small detail to the reader
One that is written for children
qs.why: The teacher says the ending asks the reader to do some of the work.

qs.q: How does Jisoo's opinion change?
o: She sees the ending fits the story's central concern.
She decides the author made a serious mistake in the ending.
She wants to write a new ending.
She asks to read a different book.
qs.why: She realises the story was about trying the handle, so the ending is complete.

qs.q: The teacher's last sentence suggests that
o: understanding and liking are two separate matters
readers must always enjoy every open ending they read
teachers choose the endings of books
stories should never end clearly
qs.why: The teacher separates comprehension from personal taste.

items.title: Comparing a Film and the Book
items.text:
Hyun: Have you seen the film of "The Glass Orchard"?
Dana: Last weekend. I read the novel first, so I was disappointed.
Hyun: Really? I liked the film more. The orchard looks beautiful on screen.
Dana: It does, but the book spends a hundred pages on the narrator's thoughts, and the film has almost none of them.
Hyun: Maybe that is not possible in a film. A camera shows faces, not thoughts.
Dana: True, but they changed the ending. In the novel, the sisters never speak again.
Hyun: Yes, and in the film they hug. It felt too neat to me as well.
Dana: So you agree with me!
Hyun: In part. I think the director wanted a hopeful message for a wide audience.
Dana: That may be, but the sad ending was what made the book honest.
Hyun: Perhaps we should say the two works are not trying to do the same thing.

qs.q: What is the main topic of the conversation?
o: Differences between a novel and its film version
The best way to grow an orchard in a cold climate
A plan to visit the cinema
The history of glass making
qs.why: They compare how the book and the film treat the narrator's thoughts and the ending.

qs.q: Why does Dana prefer the book?
o: It gives the narrator's thoughts and a truer ending.
It is shorter than the film and much easier to read quickly.
It has more beautiful pictures.
It was written by her friend.
qs.why: She mentions the hundred pages of thoughts and says the sad ending made the book honest.

qs.q: According to Hyun, why might the film ending be different?
o: The director wanted a hopeful message for many viewers.
The actors refused to say several of the lines in the script.
The studio ran out of money.
The book was out of print.
qs.why: Hyun suggests the director aimed at a wide audience with a hopeful message.

qs.q: What does Hyun mean by "A camera shows faces, not thoughts"?
o: Film cannot easily show inner thoughts as a book can.
Cameras are not good at filming faces in poor evening light.
Actors should not show emotion.
Books have better covers than films.
qs.why: He points out a limit of the medium: a camera records what is outside, not inner thoughts.

qs.q: Which statement best summarises their final position?
o: The book and the film may have different aims.
The film is wrong and the book is right in every way.
Neither work deserves attention.
Both works have the same ending.
qs.why: Hyun's last line proposes that the two works aim to do different things, a balanced view.

items.title: An Interview With a Young Poet
items.text:
Host: Today my guest is Leila Moreno, whose first collection of poems appeared this spring. Leila, welcome.
Leila: Thank you. It is strange to hear it described as a "collection". Most of the poems began on bus tickets.
Host: On bus tickets?
Leila: I commute for two hours a day. If a line comes to me, I write it on whatever I have. Later I find it in my coat pocket, and it is a stranger's handwriting, even though it is mine.
Host: Many of your poems are very short. Is that deliberate?
Leila: Yes. I think a short poem is like a small window. You cannot put the whole house in it, so you must choose carefully what the reader sees.
Host: What do you hope readers take away?
Leila: Not a lesson. I would be happy if someone read one poem and then looked out of a bus window differently.
Host: A lovely goal. Thank you for your time.

qs.q: Where did most of Leila's poems begin?
o: On bus tickets while she was commuting
In a university classroom during the long winter term
During a stay in a mountain cabin
At the radio station
qs.why: She says most of the poems began on bus tickets during her daily commute.

qs.q: What does Leila mean when she compares a short poem to a small window?
o: The poet must choose carefully what to show.
Short poems are easier to write.
Poems are best written while sitting near a bright window.
A poem needs a frame made of glass.
qs.why: A small window shows only part of the house, so the poet selects what the reader will see.

qs.q: What is Leila's hope for her readers?
o: That a poem changes how they notice small things
That they will memorise every line
That they will learn one clear moral from every poem she wrote
That they will buy several copies
qs.why: She wants a reader to look out of a bus window differently after reading, rather than receive a lesson.

qs.q: Why does she describe her own handwriting as "a stranger's"?
o: She has forgotten writing it by the time she finds it.
She is quoting a poem by another writer.
Someone else copies her notes onto fresh bus tickets at night.
She cannot read English.
qs.why: Because the line is found later in a pocket, it seems to come from someone else, showing the distance between the moment of writing and the finding.

items.q: Read the line: "The classroom was a zoo by noon." Which figure of speech is used?
o: Metaphor
Simile
Alliteration
Onomatopoeia
items.why: The classroom is directly said to be a zoo, without "like" or "as", so it is a metaphor.

items.q: Which sentence contains a simile?
o: Her voice was as smooth as warm honey.
Time is a thief that steals our best years.
The wind whispered through the trees.
Peter Piper picked a peck of peppers.
items.why: A simile compares two things using "as" or "like"; the first sentence uses "as smooth as".

items.q: In the line "The old house sighed and settled into the night", the house is given a human action. This device is called
o: personification
hyperbole
situational irony
understatement
items.why: Giving human qualities, such as sighing, to a non-human object is personification.

items.q: "I have told you a million times to close the window!" The phrase "a million times" is an example of
o: hyperbole
understatement
rhyme
flashback
items.why: It is a deliberate exaggeration to stress feeling, which is hyperbole.

items.q: Which line is an example of alliteration?
o: Sally sells silver shells by the shore.
The door creaked loudly and then slammed shut again.
He ran as fast as a hare.
All the world's a gentle dream.
items.why: The repeated /s/ sound at the beginning of several words (Sally, sells, silver, shells, shore) is alliteration.

items.q: The words "buzz", "crash" and "hiss" imitate sounds. This device is called
o: onomatopoeia
irony
foreshadowing
metaphor
items.why: Words that imitate the sounds they describe are onomatopoeia.

items.q: A fire station is destroyed by fire on the day of its opening. What kind of irony is this?
o: Situational irony
Verbal irony
Dramatic irony
Poetic irony of sound
items.why: The outcome is the opposite of what we expect; this is situational irony.

items.q: Watching a storm, someone says "What lovely weather!" while the rain pours into her shoes. The speaker is using
o: verbal irony
personification
alliteration
foreshadowing
items.why: She says the opposite of what she means, which is verbal irony.

items.q: In a story, the narrator mentions early on that the bridge "looked a little weaker each day". Later the bridge falls. The early hint is an example of
o: foreshadowing
flashback
hyperbole
dramatic symbolism
items.why: A hint about later events is foreshadowing.

items.q: "A deafening silence filled the room." The phrase joins two opposite ideas. It is an example of
o: an oxymoron
an onomatopoeia
an alliteration
a rhyme
items.why: A phrase that joins contradictory terms, such as deafening silence, is an oxymoron.

items.q: In a poem, a white dove appears at the end of a war. The dove most likely stands for
o: peace
winter
danger
wealth
items.why: In literature a white dove is a traditional symbol of peace.

items.q: "Opening that old trunk was like opening Pandora's box." This phrase assumes the reader knows a famous story from Greek myth. This device is called
o: allusion
rhyme
alliteration
onomatopoeia
items.why: A brief reference to a well-known person, event or story is an allusion.

items.q: "The fog crept in on little cat feet" gives us a picture of the fog's soft, silent movement. The picture created in the reader's mind is called
o: imagery
plot
rhythm
dialogue
items.why: Language that appeals to the senses to form a mental picture is imagery.

items.q: In a story, the main character who wants something and drives the action is called the
o: protagonist
narrator
antagonist
secondary character
items.why: The protagonist is the central character of the story.

items.q: In a detective story, Inspector Reed tries to catch a clever thief who always escapes. The inspector is the protagonist. Who is the antagonist?
o: The thief who works against the inspector
The inspector who follows the thief's clues
The reader who tries to guess
The author who wrote the story
items.why: The antagonist is the force or character that opposes the protagonist; here the inspector is the protagonist and the thief opposes him.

items.q: Which part of the plot contains the greatest tension, the point where the outcome is decided?
o: The climax
The exposition
The resolution
The title
items.why: The climax is the peak of tension and turning point of the story.

items.q: Which element of a story do the words "a foggy harbour town in the 1920s" mainly describe?
o: The setting
The theme
The conflict
The point of view
items.why: Time and place make up the setting.

items.q: "I knew the stairs would creak, so I stepped around the third one." Which point of view is used?
o: First person
Second person
Third-person limited
Third-person omniscient
items.why: The narrator uses "I", which is first-person narration.

items.q: A narrator who knows every character's thoughts, as in "Anna feared the test while Tom secretly wished she would fail", has
o: an omniscient point of view
a first-person point of view
a second-person point of view
a limited point of view
items.why: Access to the thoughts of several characters shows an omniscient narrator.

items.q: A story pauses and shows events from ten years earlier to explain a character's behaviour. This technique is called
o: a flashback
a sudden climax
a rhyme
a stanza
items.why: Moving back to earlier events is a flashback.

items.q: A story shows a boy who gives up his last coin to help a stranger, and later he is helped in return. Which sentence states a possible theme?
o: Kindness often comes back to those who give it.
Boys should save their coins.
Strangers are always dangerous and should never be helped.
The story takes place in a market.
items.why: A theme is a general idea about life; the first sentence states such an idea, while the others are advice, a mistaken idea, or setting.

items.q: A group of lines in a poem, separated from the next by a space, is called a
o: stanza
chapter
scene
paragraph
items.why: Poems are divided into stanzas.

items.q: In a four-line poem the last words of the lines are "light", "day", "night", "way". What is the rhyme scheme?
o: AABB
ABAB
ABBA
ABCD
items.why: Lines 1 and 3 rhyme (light, night) and lines 2 and 4 rhyme (day, way), so the pattern is ABAB.

items.q: A poem of fourteen lines, usually with a fixed rhyme pattern, is a
o: sonnet
limerick
ballad
riddle
items.why: A sonnet has fourteen lines.

items.q: Two consecutive lines that rhyme and complete a thought, such as "The night was long, the stars were few; / I walked alone and thought of you", form a
o: couplet
stanza of six lines
sonnet
haiku
items.why: Two successive rhyming lines make a couplet.

items.q: The regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a poem is called
o: rhythm (meter)
the plot structure
setting
dialogue
items.why: Rhythm or meter describes the pattern of stress in poetry.

items.q: In a play, a character alone on stage speaks his thoughts aloud so that the audience can hear them. This speech is a
o: soliloquy
narrative prologue
stanza
caption
items.why: A soliloquy is a speech by a lone character revealing inner thoughts.

items.q: In a script, the line "(She slams the door.)" is a
o: stage direction
title of the play
theme
rhyme
items.why: Words in brackets that describe action are stage directions.

items.q: "The empty swings creaked in the grey drizzle, and nobody came to the park all afternoon." The mood of this sentence is best described as
o: lonely and gloomy
excited and joyful
angry and violent
silly and playful
items.why: Empty swings, grey drizzle and nobody around create a lonely, gloomy mood.

items.good: By the time the rescuers arrived, the old keeper had already left the island.
items.ko: 구조대가 도착했을 때 늙은 관리인은 이미 섬을 떠난 뒤였어요.
bad: By the time the rescuers arrived, the old keeper had already leave the island.
By the time the rescuers arrived, the old keeper had already leaving the island.
By the time the rescuers arrived, the old keeper have already left the island.

cz.st: By the time the rescuers arrived, the old keeper had already ___ the island.

items.rule: 이야기에서 다른 과거 시점보다 먼저 일어난 일은 과거완료(had + 과거분사)로 나타내요.

items.good: Never had she heard a silence so heavy.
items.ko: 그녀는 그렇게 무거운 침묵을 들어 본 적이 없었어요.
bad: Never she had heard a silence so heavy.
Never had heard she a silence so heavy.
Never she heard had a silence so heavy.

cz.st: Never ___ she heard a silence so heavy.

items.rule: 부정 부사(never)가 문장 앞에 오면 조동사가 주어 앞으로 가는 도치가 일어나요. 문학 작품에서 강조하려고 자주 쓰여요.

items.good: If I were the narrator, I would trust the old man less.
items.ko: 내가 화자라면 그 노인을 덜 믿을 거예요.
bad: If I am the narrator, I would trust the old man less.
If I were the narrator, I will trust the old man less.
If I would be the narrator, I would trust the old man less.

cz.st: If I ___ the narrator, I would trust the old man less.

items.rule: 현재 사실과 반대되는 가정은 'If + 주어 + were ..., 주어 + would + 동사원형'으로 나타내요.

items.good: Not only does the poem rhyme, but it also tells a story.
items.ko: 그 시는 운을 맞출 뿐만 아니라 이야기도 들려줘요.
bad: Not only the poem does rhyme, but it also tells a story.
Not only the poem to rhyme, but it also tells a story.
Not only does the poem rhymes, but it also tells a story.

cz.st: Not only ___ the poem rhyme, but it also tells a story.

items.rule: Not only가 문장 앞에 오면 'does + 주어 + 동사원형'처럼 도치되고, does 뒤의 동사는 원형이에요.

items.good: The writer whose poems we studied was born in a small village.
items.ko: 우리가 공부한 시를 쓴 작가는 작은 마을에서 태어났어요.
bad: The writer who poems we studied was born in a small village.
The writer which poems we studied was born in a small village.
The writer whom poems we studied was born in a small village.

cz.st: The writer ___ poems we studied was born in a small village.

items.rule: 소유를 나타내는 관계대명사는 whose이고, 뒤에 명사(poems)가 바로 와요.

items.good: Having finished the novel, she wrote a short review.
items.ko: 그 소설을 다 읽은 뒤에 그녀는 짧은 서평을 썼어요.
bad: Having finish the novel, she wrote a short review.
Having finishing the novel, she wrote a short review.
Having been finished the novel, she wrote a short review.

cz.st: Having ___ the novel, she wrote a short review.

items.rule: 주절보다 앞서 일어난 일은 분사구문 'Having + 과거분사'로 나타내요.

items.good: The ending was so surprising that several readers gasped.
items.ko: 결말이 너무 놀라워서 여러 독자가 숨을 헉 들이마셨어요.
bad: The ending was too surprising that several readers gasped.
The ending was so surprising what several readers gasped.
The ending was such surprising that several readers gasped.

cz.st: The ending was ___ surprising that several readers gasped.

items.rule: 'so + 형용사 + that ~'은 '너무 ~해서 …하다'는 뜻이에요. such 뒤에는 명사가 와요.

items.good: The detective must have known that the butler was lying.
items.ko: 탐정은 집사가 거짓말을 하고 있다는 것을 알았음이 틀림없어요.
bad: The detective must have know that the butler was lying.
The detective must has known that the butler was lying.
The detective must had known that the butler was lying.

cz.st: The detective must ___ known that the butler was lying.

items.rule: 'must have + 과거분사'는 과거 일에 대한 강한 추측을 나타내요. must 뒤에는 항상 동사원형이 와요.
